title: The CAP Theorem, Simply
intro: In a distributed system, network problems are unavoidable. CAP describes the choice you must make when they happen.

slides.heading: C, A and P
slides.subtitle: Three properties.
slides.explain: Consistency: every read sees the latest write. Availability: every request gets a response. Partition tolerance: the system keeps working when links between nodes fail.
points: C: everyone sees the same data
A: every request gets an answer

slides.heading: The real choice
slides.subtitle: During a partition, pick C or A.
slides.explain: Networks do fail, so distributed systems must tolerate partitions. When one happens, a cut-off node must either refuse requests or answer with possibly stale data.
points: CP: refuse rather than be wrong

slides.heading: CP systems
slides.subtitle: Correctness first.
slides.explain: CP systems return an error or wait rather than show outdated data. Choose this when wrong data is worse than no data.

slides.heading: AP systems
slides.subtitle: Always respond.
slides.explain: AP systems keep serving and sync up later, which is called eventual consistency. Choose this when staying up matters more than being perfectly current.

slides.heading: Eventual consistency
slides.subtitle: Correct, just not instantly.
slides.explain: Copies may disagree for a short time, but they converge once updates spread. For likes or view counts, a short delay is fine.

scenario.situation: A ticketing site lets two data centers sell seats independently during a network split.
scenario.problem: Both sides keep selling, and the same seat is sold to two different people.
scenario.fix: Treat seat booking as CP: if a data center can't confirm with the other, it pauses sales instead of risking a double booking.
scenario.takeaway: Choose consistency where mistakes are costly.

cta: Would you pick CP or AP for a chat app, and why?
